screens.title: Data Models and YANG
screens.subtitle: Why structured models replace brittle CLI parsing and how YANG defines network schemas

narration.text: In modern network automation, relying on parsing free-form command line output becomes a liability. Structured data models provide a formal blueprint for device configuration and operational state so your automation is predictable, validated, and maintainable. In this lesson we focus on YANG, the widely adopted modeling language that describes configuration, state, RPCs, and notifications in a hierarchical, machine-readable way. You will learn the core building blocks — modules, containers, lists, leaves, and types — and how they map to programmatic payloads you send with NETCONF or RESTCONF. We will also walk through a simple YANG module for interfaces and show how tools like pyang help you inspect a model as a readable tree. Along the way, you’ll see common beginner mistakes, such as trying to memorize every keyword instead of internalizing the conceptual roles of containers versus leaves, and practical checks like distinguishing config true from config false. By the end of the chapter you will be able to read a basic YANG module, locate list keys, explain why lists map to arrays of objects, and prepare simple JSON or XML payloads for automation. Consider this a foundation: the mental model you build here is what lets you move from brittle CLI parsing to reliable, model-driven automation.

keyIdea.title: Why YANG matters
keyIdea.text: YANG defines a machine-readable schema for device configuration and state, enabling predictable automation and validation across vendor platforms.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Data Models and YANG
Data Models and YANG
Structured schemas for configuration and state; a reliable bridge to automation.
Orientation

You will learn why data models replace brittle CLI parsing, how YANG describes hierarchies of containers, lists and leaves, and how to use tools to validate and explore models before building API payloads.

What you'll do

Read a YANG module, identify containers and list keys, run a pyang tree view, and craft a JSON payload for a VLAN list. These are practical skills you can apply to device APIs.

Explore Key Topics
Data Models
Formal schemas that define types, constraints, and relationships so automation can validate inputs.
YANG Language
Human-readable, tree-structured definitions for modules, containers, lists, and leaves.
Tools
Use validators like pyang to inspect tree views and catch model errors before runtime.
Visual Concept
Module
Top-level schema unit with namespace
Container
Groups related nodes, like a folder
Leaf
A single typed value, like name or address
Quick start
Start by reading a model and running a validator. The rest of this lesson breaks that workflow into small, practical steps so you can practice safely on real device models.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Foundational skills and conceptual understanding you will gain

narration.text: These objectives frame what you should be able to do after completing this chapter. First, you will understand why structured data models are essential: they formalize what can be configured, what types are allowed, and how values relate. That understanding prevents brittle scripts that rely on fragile CLI parsing. Second, you will be able to describe the fundamental role of the YANG language: it provides a human-readable, hierarchical description of configuration and state and separates the schema from the encoding format. Third, you will identify core YANG components such as module, container, list, leaf, leaf-list and type, and explain their roles during automation. Fourth, you will interpret a basic YANG module and trace how a list key uniquely identifies entries. Each objective is measurable: you should be able to point to elements in a model, explain their function, and reason about how they map to a JSON or XML payload. These skills reduce errors and help you validate payloads before sending them to devices.

screens.title: What is a Data Model?
screens.subtitle: Formal schemas that structure configuration and state for reliable automation

narration.text: A data model is a formal, machine-readable description of what data exists on a device, how it is organized, and what constraints apply. Think of it as a blueprint: it names nodes, specifies types like integer or string, sets valid ranges, and shows relationships between nodes. This formal description lets machines validate inputs and understand what to expect from device state. For example, instead of parsing a vendor CLI output string for an interface speed, a model describes an interface leaf with type enumeration or integer and a well-known path to that leaf. A practical benefit is predictability: your automation can verify that a payload conforms to the model before sending it, avoiding misconfigurations caused by unexpected CLI formats. A common misconception is to treat models as mere documentation; instead treat them as executable contracts — they can be enforced by validators and used to generate A P I payload schemas. To ground this idea, imagine a house blueprint: rooms are containers, repeated rooms like hotel suites are lists, and windows or doors are leaves. This analogy keeps roles clear and prevents the trap of memorizing keywords; focus on structure and purpose. How would treating a model as a contract change the way you validate automation payloads?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A data model is a machine-readable blueprint that enforces types, constraints and relationships for configuration and state.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › What is a Data Model?
Definition and role

A formal, machine-readable description of device configuration and operational state that enforces types and relationships so automation behaves predictably.

Why it matters
  • Enables validation of payloads before applying configuration.
  • Prevents brittle scripts that parse vendor-specific CLI output.
  • Defines a contract for automation and tooling across device families.
Key Takeaway

Treat models as executable contracts, not just documentation. Validate against them before applying changes.

Blueprint analogy
Rooms are containers, repeated rooms are lists, and individual features like windows or doors are leaves. This mapping helps you reason about hierarchy and keys when converting models to payloads.
Common misconception

Many learners try to memorize keywords. Instead, understand conceptual roles: containers group, lists repeat, leaves hold values. That mental model is more durable across vendor models.

Try this

When you open a model, first find the top-level container, then any lists and their keys. Ask: which nodes are writable configuration versus read-only state?

screens.title: What is YANG?
screens.subtitle: A human-readable modeling language for network configuration and state

narration.text: YANG stands for Yet Another Next Generation and is the de facto modeling language used in network automation. It is a human-readable, hierarchical language used to describe configuration data, operational state, RPCs and notifications for devices. Importantly, YANG defines structure and constraints but not the wire encoding; XML or JSON express the actual data instances. Because YANG is tree-oriented, it maps naturally to device configuration hierarchies — modules define namespaces, containers group related nodes, lists represent multiple instances, and leaves hold typed values. A practical example is an interface module with a list keyed by interface name; automation can iterate that list to configure or read each interface. A frequent beginner confusion is assuming YANG prescribes an encoding; it does not — YANG is the schema. Tools parse YANG to generate schemas for encodings, validators, or documentation. Mastering YANG means reading model layout, recognizing keys, and using those keys to craft A P I payloads. Think of YANG as the grammar and structure you use to speak to devices safely and predictably. How would you explain the difference between a schema and an encoding to a teammate?

keyIdea.title: YANG summary
keyIdea.text: YANG is a schema language that describes the structure, types and constraints of network configuration and state, not the encoding itself.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › What is YANG?
Language purpose

Describe configuration, state, RPCs and notifications in a tree structure. YANG provides constraints, types and documentation strings to make models machine-actionable.

Key properties
  • Human-readable, IETF-standard language for network schemas.
  • Separates schema from encoding; models map to XML/JSON payloads.
  • Supports types, derived types, presence, defaults and constraints.
Misconception

YANG is not an API or encoding. It's the schema used to validate and generate API payloads.

Practical example

A YANG interface list keyed by name lets automation iterate over each interface instance to set description, IPs, or administrative state. The model documents valid types and defaults so your code can prepare correct values.

Check your understanding

When you open a model, ask: does this node have children (container/list) or a value (leaf)? Is the list keyed, and what is the key leaf used to identify instances?

screens.title: YANG Module Anatomy
screens.subtitle: Namespaces, prefix, revision, and top-level containers

narration.text: A YANG module is the top-level unit that groups a related set of definitions and assigns a namespace to avoid naming collisions. Typical headers include module name, namespace, prefix, organization, contact, description, and revision statements. The module then defines top-level schema nodes such as containers or lists which group the module's data. For example, a module for interfaces might include a top-level container called interfaces that holds a list of interface entries. Revision statements provide history so tools can match model versions to device software. A common pitfall is using a model without checking its revision; models evolve and a mismatch can lead to configuration errors. In practice, when you inspect a module, note the namespace and prefix — these are used by tooling and by generated documentation. Understanding module headers also helps you find vendor-specific models such as a Cisco IOS XE native module and compare them to standard models. Ask yourself: which revision matches the device software you plan to automate? YANG Module Anatomy means modules package schema elements and declare a namespace and revision, which helps match models to device versions.. In practical terms, namespaces, prefix, revision, and top-level containers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Module anatomy
keyIdea.text: Modules package schema elements and declare a namespace and revision, which helps match models to device versions.

  • organization and contact — helpful for vendor models.
  • revision statements — always confirm the model revision against your device.
Practical tip

Use the namespace and revision to pick the right YANG file for your device software version.

Top-level nodes

Modules expose top-level containers or lists that map to logical groupings, such as interfaces or VLANs. Finding these top-level nodes gives you the starting path for building payloads.

Quick checklist

  • Locate the top-level container or list for your target configuration.
  • Identify any imports or typedefs referenced by the module.

screens.title: Containers, Lists, Leaves and Types
screens.subtitle: The primary nodes that make up a YANG model tree

narration.text: The core nodes in a YANG schema are containers, lists, leaves and leaf-lists. A container is an interior node that groups related child nodes but has no value itself. A list represents repeated instances of similar objects and is identified by one or more key leaves; for example, an interface list keyed by name. A leaf is a terminal node that holds a single typed value such as a string, integer, boolean or enumeration. A leaf-list allows multiple values of a single type. Types define what values are allowed, and YANG offers built-in primitives as well as derived types. Presence containers add semantic meaning when the container’s presence itself indicates configuration. A frequent error is confusing a container for a writable leaf; containers group nodes while leaves hold actual configuration values. When building automation, translate lists to arrays of objects keyed by the list key and map leaves to fields in each object. As a quick mental test, open a model and ask: which nodes would I need to create to represent an instance in JSON? That practice helps you convert schema to payload reliably.

keyIdea.title: Building blocks
keyIdea.text: Containers group, lists repeat identified entries, leaves hold values, and types constrain those values.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Core Building Blocks
Container

Groups related child nodes. No value itself; acts like a folder in the schema tree.

List

A sequence of entries keyed by one or more leaves. Map to arrays of objects in JSON with each object containing the key field.

Leaf / Leaf-list

Leaves hold single typed values. Leaf-lists hold repeated typed values such as multiple DNS servers.

Types and attributes

Types constrain allowed values. Attributes such as presence, mandatory, default and config guide validation and behavior.

Example mapping

A YANG list named vlan keyed by id becomes JSON: {"vlan": [{"id":10,...},{"id":20,...}]}. Always place the key leaf in each list object.

screens.title: Example: example-interface.yang
screens.subtitle: Read a simplified module to identify module, container, list, leaves and attributes

narration.text: Let's walk through the provided example-interface. yang to practice identifying elements. The module header declares namespace, prefix, organization and revision — metadata you should check first. Inside, a top-level container interfaces holds a list called interface. The list has key "name" so each entry is uniquely identified by that leaf. Within each interface entry you find leaves such as name, description and enabled, and a child container called ipv4 that itself holds address and netmask leaves. Notice attributes: presence on the ipv4 container indicates that enabling IPv4 is meaningful, and enabled has a default true. When you read this model, mark which nodes you will include in a payload to create or modify an interface: the list entry must include the key name and any configuration leaves you intend to set, like description or ipv4/address. A common misunderstanding is expecting defaults to always be present in the payload; defaults are applied by the device if the leaf is omitted. When preparing automation, include keys and explicitly set values for non-default behavior. Which nodes would you include to add an interface with a specific IPv4 address?

keyIdea.title: Read a model
keyIdea.text: Identify module header, containers, list keys and leaves so you can build correct payloads for each instance.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Example: example-interface.yang
Module excerpt
module example-interface {
  namespace "urn:example:interface";
  prefix "ex-if";

  container interfaces {
    list interface {
      key "name";

      leaf name {
        type string;
      }

      leaf description {
        type string;
        mandatory false;
      }

      container ipv4 {
        presence "IPv4 is enabled on this interface.";

        leaf address {
          type string;
        }
        leaf netmask {
          type string;
        }
      }

      leaf enabled {
        type boolean;
        default true;
      }
    }
  }
}
Walkthrough notes
  • module header: check namespace and revision before use.
  • list interface: key "name" means each entry must include that leaf.
  • ipv4 presence: the container's presence carries meaning; its children are relevant only when present.
  • enabled default: if omitted, device treats it as true unless explicitly set otherwise.
Example

To create an interface with IPv4, include list key name and the ipv4/address and netmask leaves inside that list entry.

screens.title: List Keys, Presence and Defaults
screens.subtitle: How keys, presence containers and default values affect payloads

narration.text: Three attributes in YANG often change how you prepare a payload: list keys, presence, and defaults. List keys uniquely identify instances; without the key you cannot target a specific list entry. For example, the interface list with key name requires each object to include a name leaf. Presence is used on containers to indicate that the container's existence itself is meaningful; when a container has presence, creating it signals intent, even if some children are omitted. Defaults supply values when a leaf is not provided; they are device-applied and do not need to be sent unless you want a different value. A common mistake is omitting a list key or assuming presence containers behave like normal empty containers. When crafting JSON or XML payloads, always include list key leaves and explicitly create presence containers when enabling a feature. As a concrete example, to enable IPv4 for interface GigabitEthernet0/1 you would include a list entry with name "GigabitEthernet0/1" and an ipv4 container with address and netmask leaves. This ensures the device receives both the identity and the configuration intent. After preparing a payload, validate it against the model to catch missing keys or type mismatches.

keyIdea.title: Payload rules
keyIdea.text: Always include list keys, create presence containers to indicate intent, and rely on defaults only when they match your desired configuration.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › List Keys & Presence
List key rule

Every list entry identified by a key must include the key leaf in the payload so the device knows which instance you mean.

Presence containers

Presence indicates the container's existence carries meaning. Create the container in your payload to signal intent to enable the feature.

Defaults and omission

Defaults are applied by the device when you omit a leaf. Don’t rely on a default if you require a specific behavior — set it explicitly.

Concrete example
{
  "interface": [{
    "name": "GigabitEthernet0/1",
    "ipv4": {"address":"192.0.2.10","netmask":"255.255.255.0"}
  }]
}

screens.title: Using pyang to Inspect and Validate Models
screens.subtitle: A short workflow to render tree views and catch syntax issues

narration.text: pyang is a practical tool for validating and visualizing YANG modules. The basic workflow is: install pyang with pip if needed, point it at the YANG file, and render a tree view or run a validator. The tree output gives a readable, hierarchical listing of containers, lists and leaves so you can quickly find the top-level node you need. For example, running pyang -f tree on a VLAN module will show a vlan-list with entries keyed by id and leaves such as name and state. Use pyang to detect syntax errors, unresolved imports or missing typedefs before attempting to use the model in automation. A common beginner step is to skip this validation and then wonder why an A P I call fails — validating early saves time. When exploring a vendor model, run pyang -f tree and then search for the list name and key you plan to use. This habit ensures you know the exact schema path and avoids accidental writes to operational state nodes. Which model will you inspect first with pyang to practice this workflow? Using pyang to Inspect and Validate Models means install pyang, run tree rendering for readability, and validate modules to find errors before using them in automation.. In practical terms, a short workflow to render tree views and catch syntax issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Validation workflow
keyIdea.text: Install pyang, run tree rendering for readability, and validate modules to find errors before using them in automation.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Using pyang
Install and run
pip install pyang
pyang -f tree cisco-ios-xe-vlan.yang

The command renders a concise tree so you can find lists, keys and leaves quickly.

Inspecting output
module: Cisco-IOS-XE-vlan
  +--rw vlan-list
     +--rw vlan* [id]
        +--rw id         uint16
        +--rw name?      string
        +--rw state?     enumeration

Search this output for the list name and key to determine how to construct payloads.

screens.title: Configuration vs Operational State
screens.subtitle: Understanding config true and config false nodes

narration.text: A critical distinction in YANG is between configuration data and operational state. Nodes with config true, the default, represent writable configuration you can change. Nodes with config false represent operational or read-only state populated by the device — you should not attempt to write them. Confusing these leads to failed A P I calls or unexpected behavior. For example, a vlan's operational state might include dynamic counters or status fields marked config false; these are useful for monitoring but not for setting. When designing automation, separate flows that write configuration from flows that read state. Validate models for config attributes: pyang tree output and vendor documentation will show which nodes are config false. Another common error is assuming the presence of a leaf implies you can change it — always check the config attribute. A practical rule: if you plan to send NETCONF or RESTCONF payloads, target nodes explicitly marked as configuration and avoid state-only nodes. How will you separate read and write paths in your automation toolkit? Configuration vs Operational State means always check the config attribute: config true nodes are writable configuration, config false nodes are read-only operational state.. In practical terms, understanding config true and config false nodes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Config vs state
keyIdea.text: Always check the config attribute: config true nodes are writable configuration, config false nodes are read-only operational state.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Config vs Operational State
Config true (writable)

These nodes represent configuration you can change with NETCONF or RESTCONF. Prepare payloads that target these nodes for automated changes.

Config false (read-only)

Operational state populated by the device. Use these nodes for monitoring or verification but do not attempt to write them.

Practical guidance
  • Inspect model attributes to distinguish writable nodes from state-only nodes.
  • Separate automation into write flows (config true) and read-only monitoring flows (config false).
  • Validate payloads against the model to avoid writing to state-only nodes.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safe Practices
screens.subtitle: What learners commonly get wrong and how to avoid those traps

narration.text: When starting with YANG, learners often try to memorize every keyword and syntax detail. That approach is brittle. A better strategy is to internalize the conceptual roles — containers group nodes, lists repeat keyed entries, and leaves carry typed values — and practice mapping that structure to payloads. Another frequent mistake is not checking model revision and blindly using a model that doesn't match the device software. Always match module revision to device version to prevent mismatches. Skipping validation with tools like pyang before applying a payload is a common source of runtime errors; validate first to catch missing imports or unresolved typedefs. Finally, mixing configuration and operational state in write operations will cause failures: verify config true before writing. Safe practices include: run pyang to render a tree and confirm keys and types, prepare small test payloads targeting a single list entry, and use presence containers explicitly when you mean to enable a feature. These habits reduce risk and increase confidence when automating device changes. What small validation step will you add to your workflow today to avoid a common mistake?

keyIdea.title: Avoid mistakes
keyIdea.text: Focus on conceptual roles, check model revisions, validate with tools, and separate read and write flows to prevent errors.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Common Mistakes & Practices
Mistake: Memorize syntax

Don’t memorize keywords. Learn conceptual roles and map them to payload shapes instead.

Mistake: Skip validation

Always run pyang or similar validators to catch schema issues before applying changes.

Practice: Small tests

Apply small, controlled test payloads to a single list entry to verify behavior before wide changes.

Pro tip

Automate the validation step so every generated payload is checked against the model before being sent to the device.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Core terms and short definitions to keep handy

narration.text: Here are essential concepts to remember. First, a data model is a formal, structured description of configuration and state — treat it as a contract you can validate against. Second, YANG is the language used to write those models; it describes hierarchical schema elements and constraints but not the encoding used on the wire. Third, a module is the top-level unit in YANG that assigns a namespace and revision and contains the schema nodes you will inspect. Keep these definitions in mind as quick mental anchors when you open new models or prepare automation payloads. Summary

Keep these three concepts at hand when you inspect models: the model is the contract, YANG is the language, and module packages schema elements with a namespace and revision.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Practical reminders for working with YANG models

narration.text: These practical reminders will help you work safely. First, container groups do not hold values — leaves do. Second, lists are repeated objects identified by key leaves; map lists to arrays of objects in JSON or XML. Third, always validate models with tools like pyang and check config attributes to separate writable configuration from operational state. Remember these three checks before you automate: identify keys, confirm writable nodes, and validate the model version. These simple rules prevent common errors and make your automation more reliable. Lists and keys
